column2: They then saw the Lord, the supreme god of gods; seeing the Supreme Ruler who bears a third eye,
Shakra and the other gods, all lords of gods, understood. The goddess, delighted, in the presence of the dwellers in heaven,
of immeasurable radiance, placed a garland of flowers at his feet. All the gods again said to the Lord, "Well done, well done,"
and with their heads touching the ground bowed to him with the goddess. Then in the meantime, Brahmins, I with the deities
spoke to the radiant great mountain Himavan: "You are praiseworthy, worthy of worship and bowing to by all, great.
Your connection with Sharva is a great rise; let a lovely wedding be performed; why delay further?" Then Himavan bowed and replied to me:
You alone are the cause, god, of all my rise; my grace has arisen suddenly and you too are its reason. As the wedding should be, Grandfather, so ordain it.
Then, hearing this word of the king of mountains, Brahmins, I said to the Lord, "Let the wedding be performed, god."
Lord Shankara said to me, "As you wish, guardian of the world." And at that moment, Brahmins, we built a city
for Maheshvara's wedding, adorned with many jewels; gems, varied jewels, gold and pearls
came in embodied forms and adorned the excellent city; the floor was varied emerald, adorned with golden pillars,
with shining crystal walls, hung with pearl necklaces; at its lovely gate in the city, built for the wedding,
it shone, belonging to the god of gods, the great-souled Maheshvara; the Moon and Sun, as two great gems, heated it equally there.
The wind, carrying a delightful fragrance, blew with a pleasant touch, showing devotion to Bhava.
The four oceans were there, and the best of gods led by Shakra, divine rivers, great rivers, Siddhas and sages,
all Gandharvas and Apsarases, Nagas, Yakshas with Rakshasas, water-dwellers, sky-goers, Kinnaras, divine Charanas,
Tumburu, Narada, Haha and Huhu, and the singers of Sama, taking lovely instruments, came then to the city.
The sages, rich in austerity, told tales there sung in the Vedas, and with delighted minds muttered the holy marriage mantras.
All mothers of the world and all the gods' daughters sang joyfully at the marriage of the Supreme Lord.
The six seasons came together there, bringing pleasant scents of many kinds, standing in embodied form, "the wedding of Shankara,"
with dark-blue clouds, with peacocks delighted at the sound of mantras, crying and dancing everywhere.
Laughing with fine flickering tawny lines of lightning, adorned with cranes white as lotus-garlands,
with fresh mushrooms and plantains sprung up, creepers and trees sprouting shoots, auspicious, and resounding with hosts of frogs awakened by love for the rains' auspicious streams, greatly languid —
by the delightful cries of peacocks, causes of breaking the pride of even proud women high-minded toward their lovers, in a moment,
and the great Indra's bow, of varied and radiant lovely form, curved like a line of the moon, standing near masses of clouds, greatly adorned all around;
shaking with fragrant, lovely winds born of various flowers and water, very cool through contact with dense water, the auspicious curls of the goddesses' hair;
the moon's disc hidden by thundering clouds, grass lovely with freshly sprinkled water, eagerly gazed at by travellers' wives, with sighs smoky —
rich with the sound of swan-anklets, with high clouds like breasts, a necklace of moving lightning, with clear lotus eyes —

with swans frightened by the deep roar of dark clouds, the tips of lilies bowed by streams of clear water, her limbs all shone with the pollen of fragrant flowers: at the wedding of the mountain's daughter the rainy season appeared.
Freed of the cloud-garment, breasts like lotus buds, voice like swans' anklets, the directions' edges filled with all crops;
with broad sandbanks as hips, girdle of crying cranes, delighting with eyes dark like blossoming blue lotuses,
with lips like ripe bimba fruit, smiling with jasmine teeth, preceded by a line of body-hairs dark like a fresh creeper:
with moon-ray necklaces falling on the neck and chest, delighting the minds of all the dwellers in heaven,
speaking in sweet voice like the song of intoxicated bee-swarms, shining with earrings, lovely clusters of moving water-lilies;
bearing fingers of shoots from the branches of red ashoka, adorned with garments made of heaps of its flowers,
with feet tipped like red lotuses, nails like rows of jasmine flowers, left thigh like a plantain trunk, face like the moon —
endowed with all marks, adorned with all ornaments, touching with love like a beloved, passionate and charming:

freed from the dark-cloud garment, face like the full moon's disc, eyes like blue lotuses, breasts like lotuses opened by the sun's rays, bringing delight to hearts with a breeze fragrant with pollen of many flowers, with the sound of swans' anklets, autumn was there at the goddess's wedding.
The two seasons, Hemanta and Shishira, always flooding the directions with exceedingly cool waters, came, very radiant.
By those two seasons the best of mountains, Himavan, was attained; raining powdered frost, it quickly shone as if carrying silver.
By that rain of frost, with dense and deep cloud, the Himalaya shone then like the Milk-ocean.
The great mountain, having passed through the sequence of seasons, was like a wicked man suddenly fulfilled by the service of the good.
The mountain, with peaks covered in frost-sheets, shone like a king with great white umbrellas.
Winds that repeatedly arouse love in gods and goddesses, lotus-ponds full of clear water and adorned with flowers of lilies and lotuses —
spring, the season, came for the wedding of the teacher's daughter.
Women with the tips of their breasts slightly swelling became lovelier; lakes of water neither too hot nor cold were tinted tawny with filament powder.
The priyangu and mango trees, and also the mangoes and priyangus, seemed to rebuke each other with their clusters of blossoms.
On the white peaks of the Himalaya the tilaka trees with heaps of flowers shone, as if assembled like elders for a purpose.
Blossoming ashoka creepers clinging to sala trees shone like women with arms hanging on the necks of their lovers.
In that season, white kadamba, nipa, palms, stamala, sarala and kapittha trees,
ashoka, sarja, arjuna, kovidara, punnaga, nageshvara, karnikara, clove, tala, aloe, saptaparna, banyan, ankola and coconut,
and other trees with fruits and flowers, with very charming forms, were seen; and water-bodies with golden water, frequented by chakravakas, karandavas and swans,
with koyashti, datyuha and cranes, were seen full of lotuses, lilies and fish; and birds with bodies adorned in many ways, with brightly coloured wings, were seen on the trees.
Then, rebuking those engaged in play, they made sounds, their limbs stirred by love; at that mountain, at the wedding of the mountain's daughter, winds blew with pleasant cool bodies.
Dropping white flowers slowly from the trees, winds born from Mount Malaya blew; likewise all the holy seasons shone with their limbs mingled with one another,
whose fine marks were praised; those were there, of very charming form.
Jasmines, mutually reflecting, shone with heaps of rock-flowers sung to by hosts of intoxicated bees.
Waters were made dark blue by blue lotuses, pale by pale lotus stalks, and red by red lotuses, their petals frequented by lines of maddened bees.
Lotus groves arose everywhere: golden in some wide waters, very lovely in some continuously, with lapis-lazuli stalks in some lakes.
There were lovely pools bright with lotuses and lilies, frequented by many kinds of birds, with rows of golden steps.
The peaks of that mountain, Brahmins, with well-flowering karnikara trees standing close together, shone as if golden.
With slightly opened flowers, the patala trees became pink, and all the directions were pink, forms trembling in the breeze.
Dark arjuna trees tenfold, and blue ashoka trees, grew flowering on the mountain, vying with each other.
Forests of kimshuka, frequented by lovely cries, shone on all the slopes of the mountain.
The Himalaya's beauty with clumps of tamala trees was as if joined with masses of dark clouds lying hidden in the folds.
With abundant flowers, very broad branches, tall sandal and champaka trees and the prattling of rapturous male cuckoos, the Himalaya shone exceedingly then.

Hearing the soft, intoxicated, sweet sound of cuckoos on all sides, the blue-throated peacocks with moving wings cried more sweetly; with strength increased by their sounds, the bodiless god (Kama), flower-bow and arrows in hand, made ready to pierce the limbs of heavenly women.
Summer, with sharp sunheat and mostly little water in reservoirs, came to the Himalaya at the time of the goddess's wedding.
And it, with many trees and heaps of flowers, adorned the peaks of the frosty mountain all around.
And yet on that mountain very pleasing winds blew, fragrant of patala, wide kadamba and arjuna.
Pools, red with filaments of masses of blossoming lotuses, were thronged on their shores with sounds of ducks, swans and kadambakas.
And the kurabakas, pale with flowers, on all the mountain peaks were frequented by lines of bees.
Bakulas on the wide slopes of the mountain scattered charming flowers all around.
Thus, with all trees variegated with flowers and regions made lovely by the cries of many birds, the six seasons came, best of sages, for the prosperity of the Himalaya's daughter's wedding.
When this was thus under way, at the gathering of all beings, crowded with many instruments, I there, Brahmins,
adorned the mountain's daughter with fitting ornaments and wealth, and personally, Brahmins, led her into the city.
Then I again said to the Lord, "I am offering oblation to you in the fire, standing in the position of teacher,
if you give me the command, this rite of performance is to be done." Thus Shankara, god of gods, lord of the world, said to me:
Do, lord of gods, as indicated, as you wish. I shall do all your word, Brahma, all-pervading lord of the world.
Then I, with glad heart, quickly took kusha grass and joined the god's and the goddess's hands with the yoga-bond.
Agni himself stood there with joined palms, attended by the great mantras sung in the Shruti, embodied,
having offered as prescribed ghee, that immortal oblation, and then having made them circumambulate that whole fire,
releasing the joining of hands, together with all the deities, with mind-born sons and Siddhas, with a delighted inner self,
at the time of the wedding rite, having bowed to the bull-bannered Lord, by yoga alone, Brahmins, of those two, Uma and the Supreme Lord —
that supreme wedding took place, which the gods nowhere know. Thus all this auspicious svayamvara has been told to you; hear also the supremely wondrous wedding of the god.
in lovely lines of forests, with the cries of many birds, in holy places with sacred waters and in the hermitages of sages.
They gave him weapons and effective mantras; then the groups of sages, with Kapila, said to that Prithu:
Give food to living beings; the earth has swallowed the herbs.
Then that best of kings took up his bow and said to the earth:
Give back the herbs you have swallowed, for the welfare of the people.
Frightened, the earth said to Prithu of broad eyes:
The great herbs have been digested in me; how can I give them?
Then the angry king said again to the earth:
If you do not give them today, I shall kill you and give the great herbs myself.
Why do you kill a woman, king, being wise, best of kings? Without me, how will you support these people?
Where benefit to many results from the destruction of one, there is no fault, earth; I support the people by austerity.
I see no fault in this; I do not speak a useless word. When one is felled and the happiness of many arises, the sages declare that killing greater than a hundred horse-sacrifices.
Then the gods and the sages, soothing the best of kings, and the hosts of gods said to the goddess earth, the mother:
Earth, becoming a cow, in the form of milk give the great herbs to King Prithu; then the king will be pleased, protection of the people will be possible, and then there will be well-being.
Then, taking the form of a cow, the earth stood near Kapila, and the king, born of Vena's arm, milked the great herbs.
Where the gods with Gandharvas, the sages and the sage Kapila, great sage, (milked) the earth that had taken a cow's form, at the Narmada,
the Sarasvati, the Bhagirathi, and especially the Godavari: in all the great rivers he milked abundant milk.
Milked by Prithu, she became a river of holy water and was joined with the Gautami; that was as if wondrous.
From then on they know that holy place as Kapila-sangama; there, great-minded one, eighty-eight thousand worshipful
holy places, the groups of sages say, Narada, even by remembrance are purifying in this world, all of them in due order.
Whoever is born from her is verily her son and she his mother, no doubt here; therefore those who know the truth of the Shruti say she is not a mere woman once a child is born.
Hearing that speech of her father-in-law, Atreyi at once poured water on her husband, who had become fiery in form.
Both that couple, Brahmin, met by the water of the Ganga, and both became a couple in peaceful forms.
As Vishnu with Lakshmi, as Shankara with Uma, and as the Moon with Rohini, so then was the pair.
Flooding her husband she bore a body of water; she became the river known as Parushni, joined with the Ganga.
The merit of giving a hundred cows comes from bathing in the Parushni, and there the Angirases performed sacrifices with abundant fees.
There, the Purana-reciters say, are three thousand holy places; dear one, they know a separate sacrificial fruit on each of the two banks.
Bathing and giving there are held greater than the Vajapeya, especially at the confluence of the Ganga and the Parushni.
The merit gained by bathing, giving and the like cannot be told.
Yadu said "No" to his father Yayati, giver of ample fees; Yayati, having cursed Yadu, spoke to Turvasu, who was eager:
Turvasu also did not accept the old age given by his father; having cursed him, he said to Druhyu, "Take this old age of mine."
Druhyu too did not wish the old age, destroyer of beauty, that was given; the king said also to Anu, "Take this old age of mine."
Anu said "No"; having cursed him, he spoke to Puru. Delighted, Puru then accepted that old age of his father.
For a thousand years, as long as his father was pleased, he enjoyed the various objects to be enjoyed in youth.
Satisfied with his son's youth, Yayati enjoyed happiness. Then the son of Nahusha, the king, became satiated with all pleasures; then, joyfully calling his son Puru, he said:
I am satisfied with all pleasures through your youth, sinless one; take back your youth, son, and give me back my soiled old age.
Puru then said "No": "I am worn out by old age; father, the changes of states are hard for embodied beings to prevent.
Old age, coming by force of time, must be borne by all embodied beings; if it was taken for a teacher's benefit, how can it be abandoned?
Death is better for embodied beings than the sin of abandoning what was accepted; or else, king, I shall destroy old age by austerity."
Having said so to his father he went to the unsurpassed Ganga and on the south bank of the Gautami practised great austerity.
Then, after a long time, the god Shiva became pleased, adorned with the excellent gem of great, world-transcending virtues; the best of gods said to Puru, "What shall I give?"
Lord, my father's old age, obtained by curse, Lord of the gods — destroy it, god of gods; and free my brothers, cursed in anger by my father, from the curse, you who are worshipped by the gods.
Saying "So be it," the Lord of the world destroyed the old age that came from the curse, and made his brothers free of the curse.
From then on that holy place, which destroys old age and disease and destroys by mere remembrance untimely old age and the like,
is also famed by that name, Kalanjara. There are the holy places Yayata, Nahusha, Paura, Shaukra and Sharmishtha,
and others like them; know, greatly wise one, that there are one hundred and eight holy places there, accomplishing all success.
Bathing, giving, hearing and reciting at them quell all sins and grant enjoyment and liberation.
In whose side-glance, smile, speech and play of gesture the five-arrowed (Kama) constantly dwells — who here is not conquered by them?
When the thousand-eyed one had said "So be it," the two came to the great river and saw the great sage Vishvamitra performing austerity,
hard to assail even by Death, like Shiva with matted locks sitting on earth; for a thousand years they could not see him.
When they were far away, delighting in dance, song and flattery, the tiger among sages, seeing them, became filled with anger.
Who does not feel anger on seeing opposition? Though desireless, the mighty-armed one, laughing as it were at that Indra,
released by those two apsarases, the thousand-eyed, as if speaking, cursed them: "You two, son of Gadhi, will be in the form of liquid,
since you came here to melt me, quickly." Then, appeased by them, he granted release from the curse:
When you meet the Ganga you will have divine forms. By that curse they at once became rivers.
The pair of apsarases became two rivers; they also met each other and the Ganga at a good confluence.
Famed in all worlds, auspicious, granting enjoyment and liberation, he abides there and is seen, the giver of all success.
Bathing there and seeing him, one is freed from all bondage.
Having conquered the enemies dwelling in the nether regions, he went to the heavenly world. There, having conquered, he went to the earth, killing the Daityas who stood on the mountains,
those in the ocean, in rivers, in villages and in forests; in an animal form he killed Daityas of many shapes,
those moving in the sky, staying in the wind, and those who had gone to the world of the luminaries, with claws worse than a thunderbolt's strike and his great mane flung up,
causing Daitya women to miscarry by his roars, conquering all Rakshasas, with great roars and glances like the fire of dissolution,
he crushed the Asuras with slaps and throwing of limbs. Having thus killed many kinds, Hari went to the Gautami,
born from his own lotus-foot, delighting mind and eyes. There was a foe of the king of Dandaka, famed as Ambarya,
a warrior hard for the gods to conquer, surrounded by a great force; by him a battle occurred, very fierce, terrible and hair-raising.
